extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent applicants, PTO rulemakers, litigants, and policymakers concerned with business-method patents
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing a transitional (post-grant/oppositional) proceeding for covered business-method patents under the America Invents Act, including definitions, procedural limits, stays, estoppel, effective/sunset dates, and scope exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel following transitional proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner in a transitional proceeding, or his real party in interest, may not assert either in a civil action arising in whole or in part under section 1338 of title 28, United States Code, or in a proceeding before the International Trade Commission that a claim in a patent is invalid on any ground that the petitioner raised during a transitional proceeding that resulted in a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an affirmative bar: issues raised in the PTO transitional proceeding (if resulting in a final written decision) cannot later be re-asserted by that petitioner or its real party in interest in district court or ITC litigation. Applies to grounds raised during that specific transitional proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s institution authority limited to covered business-method patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may institute a transitional proceeding only for a patent that is a covered business-method patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitional proceedings cannot be instituted for patents that do not meet the statutory definition of a 'covered business-method patent' (see separate criterion). This is a jurisdictional/eligibility limitation on PTO rulemaking and institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations effective date and applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations issued pursuant to paragraph (1) shall take effect on the date that is 1 year after the date of enactment of this Act and shall apply to all covered business-method patents issued before, on, or after such date of enactment, except that the regulations shall not apply to a patent described in section 6(f)(2)(A) of this Act during the period that a petition for post-grant review of that patent would satisfy the requirements of section 321(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations implementing transitional review become effective one year after enactment and have broad temporal application (past, present, future patents), with a specific carve-out tied to section 6(f)(2)(A) and post-grant review timing as described by section 321(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunset of subsection and regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: This subsection, and the regulations issued pursuant to this subsection, are repealed effective on the date that is 4 years after the date that the regulations issued pursuant to paragraph (1) take effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the program is repealed 4 years after regs take effect, the rules continue to apply to any petition for a transitional proceeding that is filed prior to the repeal date (i.e., petitions filed before repeal remain governed by the program).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court stay factors when a transitional proceeding exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party seeks a stay of a civil action alleging infringement of a patent under section 281 in relation to a transitional proceeding for that patent, the court shall decide whether to enter a stay based on—(A) whether a stay, or the denial thereof, will simplify the issues in question and streamline the trial; (B) whether discovery is complete and whether a trial date has been set; (C) whether a stay, or the denial thereof, would unduly prejudice the nonmoving party or present a clear tactical advantage for the moving party; and (D) whether a stay, or the denial thereof, will reduce the burden of litigation on the parties and on the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four enumerated, non-exclusive factors guide district courts on whether to stay litigation pending PTO transitional proceedings: simplification/streamlining, status of discovery/trial schedule, prejudice/tactical advantage, and reduction of litigation burden. Courts must weigh these factors in deciding stays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory appeal and standard of review for stay decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may take an immediate interlocutory appeal from a district court’s decision under paragraph (1). The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit shall review the district court’s decision to ensure consistent application of established precedent, and such review may be de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District court stay determinations (re: transitional proceedings) are immediately appealable to the Federal Circuit, which may review de novo to ensure consistency with precedent; this provides an expedited appellate check on stay rulings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'covered business-method patent'
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of this section, the term 'covered business method patent' means a patent that claims a method or corresponding apparatus for performing data processing operations utilized in the practice, administration, or management of a financial product or service, except that the term shall not include patents for technological inventions. Solely for the purpose of implementing the transitional proceeding authorized by this subsection, the Director shall prescribe regulations for determining whether a patent is for a technological invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory definition ties covered business-method patents to data processing operations for financial products/services, but explicitly excludes 'technological inventions' and delegates to the Director (PTO) the rulemaking authority to define and identify technological inventions for program implementation. This raises scope/interpretation issues and requires PTO regs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of construction re: patent-eligible subject matter (section 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in this section shall be construed as amending or interpreting categories of patent-eligible subject matter set forth under section 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transitional proceeding and its definitions do not change or constitute an interpretation of what is patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101; courts and PTO must treat §101 jurisprudence independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 18: oppositional/post-grant review as alternate to litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 18 establishes a program to review business-method patents at the USPTO (or an oppositional/post-grant proceeding) where business-method patents can be re-examined using the best prior art as an alternative to costly litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program intended to provide lower-cost administrative review of business-method patents (using best prior art) so that businesses facing meritless or low-quality business-method patents have an administrative remedy rather than expensive district-court litigation. Support letters and debate emphasize this as a tool to weed out poor-quality business-method patents and reduce litigation costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program duration extension to prevent 'lying-in-wait'
rubrics_metrics.description: H.R. 1249 extends the transitional review program of section 18 from 4 to 8 years in duration to accommodate concerns that bad actors could 'wait out' a shorter program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer program duration (8 vs. 4 years) was specifically adopted to reduce an incentive for potential plaintiffs to delay litigation until after the program lapsed, thereby ensuring broader protection during a patent's life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope adjustment beyond class 705
rubrics_metrics.description: The House amended the definition of business-method patents to eliminate tracking solely to class 705, because some offending business-method patents are issued in other classification sections; the House change does not directly track the class 705 language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history indicates the definition was broadened slightly to capture business-method patents that might be classified outside class 705; implementers must account for cross-class issuance when identifying eligible patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access by privies / shared-interest parties
rubrics_metrics.description: H.R. 1249 allows parties who have shared interests with a sued party (privies) to bring a section 18 proceeding; an alternative amendment (Cantwell) would have eliminated access by privies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Who may bring a transitional proceeding is a contested element: the House bill permits privies to seek review (broadening access), while proposed amendments sought to limit access to only the sued parties. This affects strategic use and standing to invoke the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental examination by patent holder
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislation enables patent holders to request a supplemental examination of a patent if new information arises after the initial examination, asking the USPTO to consider, reconsider, or correct information believed to be relevant to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplemental examination is intended to allow patentees to clear up post-issuance information or errors; it does not limit the USPTO’s authority to investigate misconduct or sanction bad actors, and can strengthen patents by correcting the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party submissions during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The America Invents Act creates a mechanism for third parties to submit relevant information during the patent examination process to provide the USPTO with better information about the technology and claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-party submission is a procedural quality-improvement tool allowing public input/best prior art to enhance examination efficiency and patent quality; implementers should account for timing and format rules that the PTO will set for such submissions.
